clauses.clause: Make use of texts to build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, and/or share information and ideas (any one purpose suffices — OR list). (I/C)
clauses.note: Students use information from texts (the Patterns of the Moon anchor chart, the book Does the Sun Sleep?, and their own notes drawn from those texts) to build knowledge about why the moon seems to change shape and to share information and ideas during the Science Talk — satisfying at least two purposes in the OR list (build knowledge, share information and ideas).

verdicts.evidence: Invite students to take out their Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Remind them that they will use these notes and take turns responding to their group members' ideas.
verdicts.rationale: The standard's four purposes form an OR list; any one student-performed purpose yields full. In this lesson, students make use of multiple texts — the Patterns of the Moon anchor chart, the book Does the Sun Sleep?: Noticing Sun, Moon, and Stars Patterns, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall — to build knowledge about why the moon seems to change shape and then to share that information and ideas with classmates during a structured Science Talk. Students actively use these texts when they record personal notes on the Patterns of the Moon notes sheet ("they should record only the information that they think is most important") and then deploy those text-based notes in small-group discussion: "Invite students to take out their Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Remind them that they will use these notes and take turns responding to their group members' ideas." This satisfies at least the "build knowledge" and "share information and ideas" purposes, with the student as the actor throughout.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Make use of texts to build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, and share information and ideas. (I/C)

clauses.clause: Link ideas and information to an organizational plan. (C)
clauses.note: Students write individual notes on the Patterns of the Moon notes sheet, drawing from the anchor chart, which functions as a loose organizational plan; however, the notes are personal jottings for a talk rather than a structured linking of ideas to a formal organization plan for a composed text.

clauses.clause: Highlight ideas and information that are most relevant, useful, and impactful. (C)
clauses.note: Students are directed to identify the most important information via turn-and-talk and to record only what they think is most important on their notes sheet, which is a relevance-selection act; however, the highlighting/prioritizing is informal and teacher-guided (the teacher stars the anchor chart), and the student output is personal notes rather than a constructed text with emphasized points.

verdicts.evidence: Remind students that they need to record their notes in a way that is useful to them, maybe with pictures and only a few words, so they can read from their notes and use them as evidence in the Science Talk. They should record only the information that they think is most important.
verdicts.rationale: Both clauses are partially met. For the linking clause, students write individual notes on the Patterns of the Moon notes sheet using information from the anchor chart ("they need to record their notes in a way that is useful to them … They should record only the information that they think is most important"), which is a rudimentary form of linking ideas to a source plan; however, the notes are informal jottings for an oral Science Talk, not a structured linking of ideas to an organizational plan for a composed text. For the highlighting clause, students select the most important information during a turn-and-talk ("What information do you think is most important to know…") and then record only that information, but the prioritization is largely teacher-guided (the teacher stars the anchor chart) and the student product does not formally highlight or emphasize the most relevant points within a constructed text. The standard is tagged (C) — construction — and the lesson's construction artifact (personal notes) is thin relative to the standard's expectation of linking and highlighting within an organizational plan.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Link ideas and information to the organization plan, highlighting ideas and information that are most relevant, useful, and impactful. (C)

clauses.clause: Generate ideas for writing by engaging in discussions with others.
clauses.note: Students engage in partner discussion to generate ideas before writing their notes

verdicts.evidence: Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What information do you think is most important to know when answering the question 'Why does the moon seem to change shape?''
verdicts.rationale: Students generate ideas for their Patterns of the Moon notes through all three methods. They assess prior knowledge by discussing what they think is most important from the anchor chart (Opening A: turn-and-talk about 'What information do you think is most important'). They gather information from texts including the anchor chart, Word Wall, and Does the Sun Sleep? book (Work Time A: 'invite them to look again at Does the Sun Sleep?: Noticing Sun, Moon, and Stars Patterns and jot down what they see or hear'). They engage in discussions with elbow partners before writing (Opening A).
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Generate ideas for content by assessing prior knowledge, gathering information from texts, and engaging in discussions with others. (C)

clauses.clause: Use descriptive words (C) — the student selects and employs descriptive words in their own composed text.
clauses.note: Students are directed to use adjectives and descriptive words from anchor charts during independent Sky Notebook writing, and teacher feedback confirms a student chose the descriptive word 'glowing.' However, the directive is a reminder to consult charts, not a robust, intentional focus on selecting descriptive words; the primary instructional objective is recording observations, not crafting with descriptive language.

clauses.clause: Craft texts that engage readers (C) — the student produces a text with the purpose or effect of engaging an audience.

verdicts.evidence: Remind students to use the Prepositions anchor chart and Adjectives anchor chart, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall as necessary.
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to use descriptive words to craft engaging texts (a Construction act). In the Sky Notebook independent writing (Closing A, p. 293), students are directed to "use the Prepositions anchor chart and Adjectives anchor chart, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall" while composing their observations, and teacher feedback confirms at least one student selected the descriptive adjective "glowing." This partially meets the descriptive-words clause because the lesson's primary objective is recording scientific observations, not intentionally crafting with descriptive language — the adjective/preposition use is supportive scaffolding rather than the instructional focus. The "craft engaging texts" clause is not met: no activity in the lesson has students compose a text with the goal of engaging a reader; the writing tasks (notes sheets, Sky Notebook entries, shared writing) are all observational/informational recordings, not texts crafted for audience engagement.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Use descriptive words to craft engaging texts. (C)

verdicts.evidence: Distribute pencils and the prepared clipboards with Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Focus students on the prompt. Reread it aloud and invite them to begin writing their individual notes.
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to create texts in a teacher-selected mode, with print, digital, auditory, and visual listed as interchangeable examples (OR list — any one suffices). In Work Time A, students independently write on teacher-distributed Patterns of the Moon notes sheets: "Distribute pencils and the prepared clipboards with Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Focus students on the prompt. Reread it aloud and invite them to begin writing their individual notes." The teacher selects the print mode (pencil-and-paper notes sheet with sketches). Students also complete Sky Notebook entries in Closing A ("guide students to complete this page"), a second teacher-selected print task. Both are (C) construction acts performed by the student in a teacher-chosen mode, fully meeting the standard.

clauses.clause: Discuss texts with others in the group
clauses.note: Students participate in a Science Talk in small groups, discussing the question 'Why does the moon seem to change?' using their notes — this is discussing texts/content with others.

clauses.clause: Share individual writing with the group
clauses.note: Students use their individually written Patterns of the Moon notes sheets during the Science Talk, sharing their written notes with group members as the basis for discussion.

clauses.clause: Listen to others as they share their writing
clauses.note: Students are explicitly expected to listen to group members during the Science Talk; the lesson elicits student responses about how they will demonstrate listening, and the protocol requires turn-taking and building on others' ideas.

clauses.clause: Offer feedback on peers' writing
clauses.note: Students build onto others' ideas using sentence frames, which is responding to peers' contributions — but this is adding to a discussion, not offering evaluative feedback on the quality or content of a peer's writing. The act is adjacent to feedback but not squarely 'offering feedback on writing.'

clauses.clause: Respond to feedback received on own writing

verdicts.evidence: Remind them that they used this protocol in Lesson 6 and review as necessary using the Science Talk Protocol anchor chart.
verdicts.rationale: The lesson partially aligns with 1.P.EICC.1.e. Students discuss content in small groups during the Science Talk protocol ("Invite students to take their Patterns of the Moon notes sheet and move into pre-determined groups … Guide students through the protocol"), share their individual writing (Patterns of the Moon notes sheets) with group members, and listen as others share ("How will you show your partner you are listening to him or her?" — students respond: "use eye contact; answer the questions they ask me"). Group norms are reviewed and applied but not newly developed in this lesson, so that clause is only partially met. Students build on peers' ideas using sentence frames ("I'd like to add ___"), which is adjacent to offering feedback but does not constitute evaluative feedback on peers' writing — partially met. There is no moment where students respond to feedback received on their own writing — that clause is not met.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Participate in a community of readers and writers by developing group norms, discussing texts, sharing individual writing, listening as others share their writing, and offering and responding to feedback. (I/C)
